Further, the nsion-loaded MNs. dermal drug delivery · Nanocrystals · Controlled release · Introduction Transdermal drug delivery is considered one of the highly explored areas for the systemic delivery of drugs and immunotherapeutics due to its multiple advantages when compared to conventional oral and injectable delivery routes.
The oral route of administration is limited by poor bioavailability (Rojekar et al. 2021a, b, c, d), whereas injectables are associated with needle-stick injuries.

Injectables also possess a high possibility of adverse effects that may occur due to a transient rise in plasma drug concentrations (Rojekar et al. Transdermal drug delivery systems demonstrate the potential to overcome the aforementioned limitations that results in high patient compliance (Alkilani et al. However, owing to the poor permeability of drugs across the stratum corneum (SC), passive permeation of only a few highly lipophilic (Log P 1–3) and low-molecular-weight drugs (< 600 Da) are typically favoured.

This has triggered extensive research and paved the way for the development of drug–device-based therapeutic approaches Vol.:(0112 334567 4 76 that can effectively deliver a wide range of drugs with varying physicochemical characteristics (Vora et al. Microneedles (MNs) are minimally invasive drug delivery devices comprising multiple micron-sized projections, less than 1000 µm in height, that are positioned on a supporting baseplate.
These are also widely known as MN arrays or MN patches.

Following application on the skin, these MNs tend to puncture the SC, creating microchannels across the epidermal layer that enable the drug to access the highly vascularized dermal microcirculation, leading to its systemic absorption (Donnelly et al. The optimum short length of MNs avoids the stimulation of nerves located in the deeper tissue regions, thereby minimizing the risk of pain at the administration site.

The painless administration of MNs makes them a viable alternative to invasive hypodermic needles in achieving systemic drug delivery that enhances patient acceptability (Kaushik et al. Over the years, understanding the formulation aspects of MN-based drug delivery has gained significant improvement with studies being widely carried out in developing selfadministrable, long-acting delivery systems.
The delivery of hydrophilic drugs can be achieved through dissolving MNs (DMNs).
Dissolution of the polymeric matrix after penetration through the skin enables effective therapeutic drug delivery.

Further, water-soluble, biodegradable polymers employed in the fabrication of DMNs eliminate the risk of generating biohazardous waste as it gets completely dissolved or degraded in the skin (Vora et al. However, incorporating hydrophobic drugs in DMNs is quite challenging as it necessitates the use of organic solvents to achieve solubilisation that may weaken the matrix's structure.

Co-solvents are also associated with toxicity issues that limit its use in pre-clinical studies, where safety needs to be established at much higher doses than required for human use (Dangol et al. In order to overcome the limitation mentioned above, nanosuspension-loaded DMNs have been extensively researched for the intradermal delivery of hydrophobic drugs.

The reduction in the size of drugs to the submicron range results in the formation of a colloidally stable nanosuspension that is characterized by a high drug-loading capacity (Abdelghany et al. Further, reduction in particle size to the nanometre range results in enhancement of saturation solubility and higher drug release, which augments the drug's in vitro and in vivo performance.
Vora et al. formulated a nanosuspension of the lipophilic molecule cholecalciferol, embedded into DMNs composed of hydrophilic polymers, for enhanced transdermal delivery.

Ex vivo permeation studies in porcine skin demonstrated a significantly higher skin permeation from cholecalciferol nanosuspension-loaded DMNs in comparison to MN-free cholecalciferol nanosuspension patches (Vora et al. Further, nanosuspension-loaded DMN arrays for the delivery of etravirine, an antiretroviral drug, has been investigated Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 as a potential long-acting depot system for improving the adherence in HIV-patients, owing to its ability to be selfadministered.

In vivo pharmacokinetic studies in rats suggested a higher T , t and mean residence time in groups max 1/2 treated with etravirine nanosuspension-loaded DMNs compared to those treated with intravenous etravirine solutions, suggesting its potential to produce action over an extended period of time (Rojekar et al. Altuntas et al. has investigated a novel delivery strategy for the orally inactive drug nestorone, for use as a pericoital contraceptive in females.

The study reported the development of bilayer DMNs loaded with nestorone nanosuspension (NES-NS) as a minimally-invasive delivery system to control unintended pregnancies (Altuntaş et al. In order to overcome the nonspecific targeting of antifilariasis drugs administered through conventional routes of administration such as the oral route, Permana et al. developed nanosuspension-loaded DMNs, with ivermectin, albendazole and doxycycline as model drugs.
The dermatokinetic studies demonstrated a significant enhancement in the retention time of drugs in the dermis post-administration via MNs (Permana and McCrudden 20.
The results obtained from these studies serve as proof of concept for successfully incorporating hydrophobic drugs in DMNs, making it a viable strategy for transdermal drug delivery.

This review aim to give a detailed account of the general development and characterization methods of nanosuspensions, with a special focus on long-acting nanosuspension-loaded MNs, their development strategies, characterization methods and future clinical applications.

In vivo and in vitro studies showed increased plasma half-life, decreased tumour size and higher tolerance (Martin et al. Atorvastatin is a highly active antilipidemic drug has poor gastric solubility and around 80% systemic clearance.

Microneedles as drug delivery systems In the recent era, MN-based drug delivery systems have gained tremendous attention as a novel drug delivery strategy.
The history behind the use of MNs dates back to 100 bc where the application of MNs was explored in clinical practice.
The Chinese people used acupuncture which, though considerably different from micro-needling, had a similar mechanism that resulted in the stimulation of wound healing.

Similarly, in 1905, a German dermatologist named Dr. Ernst Kromayer treated various skin-associated issues like hyperpigmentation and scars by using motor-powered dental burs of varied sizes (Walsh 20.

It has been reported that miniature needling was explored in the 1960s and was further patented by Alza Corporation in 1971 (Tucak et al. However, the concept of MNs has grown extensively, and modified versions have now existed.
Briefly, the number of published research articles and clinical studies support the development of MNs for their versatile applications in drug delivery.
Types of microneedles (MNs) MNs have been developed in various forms such as roller, syringe, patch, lancet, and pen forms.
In terms of their structural design, they have been classified into in-plane or solid, coated, dissolving and hollow (A) and their working mechanism (B).
Reprinted from Kim et al. (20 (Copyright permission obtained) Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 out-plane forms.
In addition, the shapes of MNs vary from conical, pyramidal, and cylindrical.

However, the principal basis of classification depends on their working mechanism, which further includes the coated, solid, hollow, porous, swellable, and dissolvable MNs, as shown in Fig. Solid microneedles Solid MNs pierce the skin, creating pores through which the medication reaches the systemic circulation after absorption through the skin capillaries.

A patch loaded with a drug, as in classic transdermal drug delivery, or a semisolid topical formulation, such as an ointment, lotion, cream, and gels, as in other skin treatments, can be used to apply the formulation to the skin surface over the pores (Kim et al. 2012a, b; Rojekar et al. 2021c; Kulkarni et al. Solid MNs are fabricated with a material that has sufficient mechanical strength and requires less force for insertion into the tissues.
Some of the materials used for the fabrication of solid MNs are further discussed.

Silicon microneedles A silicon dry-etching procedure is extensively employed to manufacture short silicon MNs. Reactive ion etching using a chromium mask and isotropic etching in an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etcher are used in this procedure.
Solid MNs have also been obtained through wet etching of silicon (crystalline) with an alkaline solution.
Wet etching techniques are less expensive than dry etching (Singh et al. Isotropic dry etching and anisotropic wet etching approaches have already been coupled to circumvent this limitation.

MNs for use as neural probes have also been created by chopping up a silicon substrate to generate deep grooves in a grid pattern, followed by acid etching the pillars to produce sharp probe tips (Kim et al. In a study by Howells et al., silicon MN arrays Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 fabricated using the single-step wet etching process for transdermal delivery of insulin and hyaluronic acid demonstrated effective penetration of the active molecules across the skin without significant indentation.
In this fabrication method, the silicon wafers are coated on both sides using 2.5 µm of silicon dioxide.

The photolithography process is used to pattern devices, and the device pattern is etched into the silicon dioxide mask using ICP. The wafer is flipped, and the same procedure is repeated following which the whole wafer is submerged into alkaline solution of KOH, for about 5 h for etching.
The developed MN arrays exhibited a flux rate of 59.59 µg/cm2/h for hyaluronic acid and 1.13 µg/ cm2/h for insulin.
The slower flux rate of insulin compared to hyaluronic acid could be attributed to the differences in MN length, as relatively shorter MNs were used to deliver hyaluronic acid.

However, both insulin and hyaluronic acid demonstrated significantly higher flux rates than the control, thereby establishing the role of MNs in the effective delivery of high-molecular-weight compounds that are otherwise unable to pass the barriers of SC (Howells et al. Metal microneedles Methods used to prepare metallic MNs include laser cutting (Omatsu et al. 20, metal electroplating (Davis et al. 20, laser ablation, and wet itching.

Arrays of solid metal MNs can be directly fabricated; on the other hand, two-dimensional MN arrays are created by cutting MN into titanium metal sheets and stainless steel and further bending them out of the sheet's plane at a certain angle.
Electroplating or electroless-plating metal onto positive or negative MN molds has also been used to make two-dimensional metal MN (Fomani and Mansour 20.
Li et al. fabricated a titanium porous MN array using the modified metal injection molding technique for its potential use in transdermal drug delivery.
With an average pore diameter of 1.3 µm and a porosity of around 30.1%, the MN arrays were able to penetrate the skin without fracture.

A 27 times higher flux of calcein was achieved across the skin punctured with the metallic MN array in comparison to that achieved across intact skin (Li et al. In a similar study, stainless steel MN arrays coated with the porous polymer PLGA demonstrated successful calcein dye delivery into porcine skin with an insertion depth of 750 µm.

The polymer coating enhanced the delivery rates, as evident from the delivery of rhodamine B and lidocaine from coated MNs, demonstrating about 5-times and 25-times higher drug delivery compared to the non-coated MNs (Ullah et al. Polymer microneedles Photolithography has been used to fabricate MNs using optically curable polymers; further, they are replicated by molding using a master structure (Kathuria et al. SU-8 is a UV-curable polymer that has been widely used in the fabrication of MN. By combining micro lenses on a glass substrate with an angled rotation of the substrate, the path of UV light through the SU-8 was made to taper, resulting in MN structures with sharp tips.

PMMA has also been used in the lithography, electroplating, and molding (LIGA) process to create MN arrays, which involve angled and directional (e.g., vertical) X-ray exposure (Han et al. Because of the less optical absorption of the polymers in the UV region of 390 nm, MN as long as a few mm (millimetres) with an elevated aspect ratio, can be manufactured using a standard contact lithography instrument. 3D microstructures, including MNs, have been created using a two-photon-initiated polymerization process (Damiri et al. 2022; Pardeshi et al. Carbohydrates are being investigated as suitable polymers for the fabrication of MNs. Li et al. fabricated maltose MNs for the transdermal delivery of the human monoclonal antibody IgG. Methylene blue staining following treatment of the MNs on rat skin indicated the creation of microchannels due to disruption of the SC. Further, it was found that the delivery of IgG increased, with an increase in arrays of MNs, its length and concentration.

This serves as evidence for the potential applicability of polymeric MNs in the delivery of macromolecules (Li et al. Polymer-based dissolvable MNs can be fabricated using a wide-range of materials such as dextran, hydroxypropyl cellulose, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose and amylopectin.

DMNs employing HPMC and CMC, with donepezil as the model drug, was found to dissolve in the skin within 15 min. This can be attributed to the presence of an abundant number of hydrophilic groups that enables rapid dissolution of the MNs within seconds/minutes post-application, leading to fast delivery of the preloaded cargos (Wang et al. Further, a plethora of synthetic polymers including polylactic acid (PLA), polyglycolic acid (PGA) and polylactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) have been investigated for the fabrication of MNs. PLGA MNs were fabricated by Nguyen et al. for the delivery of methotrexate across the porcine ear and human cadaver skin.
It was found that the polymeric MNs markedly enhanced in vitro transdermal delivery compared to the untreated group (Nguyen and Banga 20.

Ceramic microneedles Micromolding and sintering techniques have been used extensively to fabricate ceramic MNs. Micromolding using an alumina slurry with a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) MN and a two-photon-induced polymerization technique has also been used to create ceramic MNs (Bystrova and Luttge 20 lithographically.

A focused laser is scanned inside a photosensitive polymer ceramic hybrid resin to cause polymerization locally in the shape of the MNs using a Galvano scanner and a micro positioning tool (Doraiswamy et al. Gittard et al. fabricated silver-coated organically modified ceramic (Ormocer®) MNs with antibacterial functionality using two-photon polymerization-micromoulding and 4 80 pulsed laser deposition.
In the first step, a master structure of the MN array on a silanized glass slip was fabricated using polyethylene glycol dimethaacrylate.

Following this, thin films of silver were deposited using pulsed laser (Gittard et al. Vallhov et al. fabricated bioceramic MN arrays to deliver the model antigen ovalbumin to antigen-presenting dendritic cells in human skin.

Ceramic (calcium sulphate) MNs with a length of 600 µm and an average pore size of 12 ± 1 µm demonstrated an in vitro release of around 90% release within 1 h. Further, ex vivo skin permeation studies demonstrated the ability of the ceramic MNs to deliver ovalbumin into CD1a+ dendritic cells, located in the epidermis of human skin, thereby suggesting the potential application of ceramics in MN-based vaccination (Vallhov et al. Microneedle rollers Most solid MN have been manufactured on flat substrates; as a result, all MNs are driven inside the skin simultaneously on a cylindrical surface, and several MNs that have been manufactured are applied to the skin like a roller.
Commercially available MN rollers can be used to treat large areas of skin.
The MN roller was developed to improve skin restoration and collagen induction for cosmetic purposes.

In addition, it also enhances skin permeability for efficient transdermal delivery (Aust et al. MN rollers were created by fabricating planar MN arrays and then applying them to the surface of cylindrical rollers or vice versa (Han et al. 2007; Kim et al. Zhang et al. fabricated a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-based DMN roller device for rapid transdermal delivery of insulin across large surface areas of the skin.
Following the administration of the insulinloaded DMN roller, an immediate hypoglycaemic effect with around 50% reduction in the original blood glucose level was attained.

The MN rollers can thus overcome the limitations of MN patches, including their inability to deliver drugs across large surface areas of skin (Zhang et al. In another study, Park et al. fabricated a polymeric MN roller by inclined rotational UV lithography that was subsequently replicated by micromolding hydrophobic PLA and hydrophilic carboxy-methyl-cellulose (CMC).

The micron-sized pores created in human and porcine cadaver skin caused a 2-fold enhancement in the amount of acetyl-salicylic acid delivered compared to that of untreated skin (Park et al. Kim et al. investigated a novel Diskneedle Therapy System (DTS™), also called as the disk MN rollers, for effective transdermal delivery of high molecular weight compounds.

It was found that the penetration of Rhodamine B across the skin of hairless rats increased in accordance with the length of the MNs (0.15 mm, 0.25 mm and 0.50 mm) (Kim et al. This can be accomplished by coating MN with a drug formulation suited for coating and dissolution.
As a result, the anticipated amount of the drug is transported to the tissue immediately after the MNs are inserted.

The amount of drug that can be coated onto the tip and shaft of the MN, i.e., the maximum medication dose that may be administered in this way, is often less than 1 mg for small MN arrays (Gill and Prausnitz 2007a).

Several coating methods are explored for coating MNs which involve dipping and spraying with an aqueous solution of surfactants that further increases the viscosity to retain more formulation in the drying process.

The coating is applied by dipping into a thick coating solution film on the surface of the roller, into microwells of the coating solution for each MN, or into a big bath of coating solution once or several times.

The coating uniformity can be improved by the utilization of excipients that reduce the surface tension of the coating solution, while the coating thickness can be increased by utilizing excipients that enhance the solution viscosity.

Additionally, a layer-by-layer coating approach is also used for MN coating (DeMuth et al. The DNA and protein molecules are also coated by dipping the oppositely charged molecules present in solution, for instance, a polymer that has a positive charge, which in turn aids the formation of a polyelectrolyte multilayer.

The main limitation of the dip coating process is the wastage of drugs due to coating on the MN shafts near the base of the MNs. In order to overcome the limitation mentioned above, Liang et al. optimized the dip-coating process with a dam board, a fixture, a roller and a limit.

Dip-coating with the fixture method demonstrated homogenous drug loading in comparison to other methods (Liang et al. The atomizer can do spray coating, and an angle gas jet can be used to spray an individual MN shaft (Chen et al. A variety of surfactants and thickening agents have been used for MN coating, including Tween 20 (Gill and Prausnitz 20, Lutrol F- 68 NF (Gill and Prausnitz 2007b), Quil- A (Chen et al. 20, PLGA (Panda et al. 20, xanthum gum (Dabholkar et al. 20, karaya gum (Kim et al. The MN coating formulation is a crucial parameter for an efficient coating process.
Consideration should be taken for controlled wetting, and uniform spreading of drug solution on the surface of the MN is essential to be achieved.
In addition, it is preferable to prepare the coating solution in water for efficient dissolution throughout the skin environment.
Notably, the dried coating should provide sufficient mechanical strength and must be compatible with the pharmaceutical manufacturing process.
Also, the effect of Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 coating on the drug needs to be observed (Gill and Prausnitz 2007a).

Fluorescein (Gill and Prausnitz 20, calcein, sulforhodamine, vitamin B, bovine serum albumin (BSA; Gill and Prausnitz 2007b), and pilocarpine (Jiang et al. 20 are a few of the small molecules that have been coated.
Pilocarpine-coated MNs were investigated by Jiang et al. for efficient drug delivery through the intrascleral route in a minimally-invasive manner.
In vitro insertion tests demonstrated the ability of the drug coating to rapidly dissolve off the MNs into the scleral tissue within 30 s after insertion.

Thus, the study serves as proof of concept for coated MNs' ability to deliver drugs to the eye via the intrascleral route (Jiang et al. Gill et al. investigated a novel micronscale dip-coating process using a GRAS coating formulation to achieve a uniform coating of MNs. The compounds, including calcein, bovine-serum albumin, sulforhodamine and vitamin B, were coated using a specially formulated coating solution.
The MNs were horizontally dipped into 20–30 µL of the coating solution, held as a droplet on the tip of a pipette.
The pipette tip was mounted horizontally in a clamp, where the MN was placed opposite to it on a micro positioner.
Immersion and withdrawal of the MN was performed manually.
By using this method, the coatings were able to be localized just to the needle shafts, enabling control over the coating process (Gill and Prausnitz 2007b).

Other macromolecules include insulin (Gill and Prausnitz 2007a), BSA (Marin and Andrianov 20, horseradish peroxidase (HRP; Andrianov et al. 20, PTH hormone (Ameri et al. 20, pancreatic ribonuclease (Saurer et al. 20, and ovalbumin (Chen et al. Dissolving microneedles It involves the delivery of a drug by encapsulation within a biodegradable, inert and water-soluble polymeric MN, followed by insertion into the skin for drug release.
Polymers used for dissolving MN include PLA, PGA, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), and polycarbonate.
This is specially designed to not leave any biohazardous waste behind after being used.
DMNs have been fabricated by using micromolds by a solvent casting process in which the polymer melt will solidify in the mold, followed by in situ polymerization of liquid monomers.

There are various construction materials that have been used, including CMC, PLGA, PVA, dextran, sugar, etc. Some of the heat-sensitive molecules like protein and peptides can be encapsulated in these MNs and solidified at moderate temperature conditions to avoid any degradation or loss of therapeutic activity.

Interestingly, CMC MNs were fabricated to avoid the formation of small voids in the MN matrix that can compromise the structure (Dangol et al. It was reported that the DMNs need to be inserted into the skin for at least 5 min for complete dissolution.
In order to enable the shortening of this time period, MNs were designed that tend to separate from the shaft within a few seconds (Chu and Prausnitz 20.
He et al. fabricated DMNs composed of hyaluronic acid and PVP-K90 to achieve enhanced dermal delivery of propranolol hydrochloride.
Since the use of hyaluronic acid alone results in high fragility of the MNs, PVP-K90 was incorporated to confer mechanical strength to the inserts.
By using the two-step casting procedure, controlled drug loading in the needle tips were achieved.

Also, the DMNs exhibited a significant enhancement in the permeability and skin retention of propranolol, as compared to the solution counterpart (He et al. Ohn et al. developed triamcinolone acetonide-loaded DMNs for enhancing therapeutic outcomes in chronic inflammatory skin diseases.

The fabricated MNs upon insertion into the skin of an inflammatory mouse model led to alleviation of inflammation by suppression of the inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine gene expression (Ohn et al. Tip-DMNs were fabricated by Chen et al. for transdermal delivery of the drug meloxicam.
In vitro release experiments demonstrated rapid release of around 91.72% of the drug within 30 min and a relative bioavailability of around 122.3% was achieved in in vivo pharmacokinetic studies.

Based on these results, it could be concluded that strong anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects can be achieved through tip-DMN arrays (Chen et al. Hollow microneedles Hollow MNs offer a well-defined strategy for drug delivery into the skin or other tissues.
Hollow MNs permit the pressure-driven flow of a liquid formulation, like hypodermic injections.
A gradual infusion or a time-varying delivery rate, pressure and flow rate can be controlled for rapid bolus injection.
The liquid formulation may make it easier to use existing injectable formulations for MN-associated drug delivery.
The hollow MNs have interesting exciting characteristics, such as incorporating the maximum possible drug dose and control over the delivery profile.
The MN design is thus simplified.

Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) are used to fabricate hollow MN, such as deep reactive ion etching of silicon, integrated lithographic molding technique, laser micromachining, deep X-ray photolithography, wet chemical etching and microfabrication have been used to fabricate hollow MNs directly from a material substrate.
Various techniques of actuating flow have been invented to induce liquid flow through hollow MN. A hollow MN is often utilized with a syringe to inject liquid formulations.

On the other hand, some hollow MN devices include an actuator (Kim et al. In a study by Yadav et al., 3D-printed hollow MN arrays were fabricated using stereolithography for efficient 4 82 transdermal delivery of rifampicin.
Oral administration of rifampicin results in chemical instability on exposure to the gastric microenvironment, low bioavailability and severe hepatotoxicity.

Fabrication of the drug in the form of hollow-MNs enables the attainment of desired therapeutic concentrations through the transdermal route, thereby overcoming the limitations mentioned above of conventional dosage forms (Yadav et al. Xenikakis et al. fabricated 3D-printed hollow MNs for effective transdermal delivery of insulin across the human skin.
By using a computer-aided design (CAD) software, two geometries of hollow MNs, namely syringe-like and pyramid MNs, were designed.

Diffusion studies demonstrated that syringe-like hollow MNs were more effective in terms of insulin delivery as compared to curved-pyramid MNs. Though the insertion force for penetration of syringe-like MNs was higher (10 N) as compared to curved-pyramid (5 N), the former was found to be more suitable for the delivery of macromolecules such as insulin, owing to its unique geometrical characteristics (Xenikakis et al. The concept of nanosuspension‑loaded microneedles High throughput screening of drug candidates through in silico methods has led to the discovery of abundant new drug molecules that can fit the hydrophobic receptor pockets well.
However, many of the recently emerging drug candidates possess a high Log P value and high molecular mass, both significant factors that contribute to insolubility.
Around half of the new drugs in the development-pipeline fail because of solubility issues.

Formulating such drugs in the form of nanosuspension-loaded MNs can not only overcome solubility-related problems but may also provide additional benefits such as enhancement in the pharmacokinetic profiles (Rabinow 2004; Mahajan et al. 2020, 2021; Fotooh Abadi et al. MN devices consist of micron-sized needles arranged in patches.

It was developed to overcome the problems associated with conventional hypodermic needles and can deliver a varied range of therapeutic moieties such as small molecules, vaccines (Menon et al. 2021; Kulkarni et al. 20, and peptides (Kirkby et al. Its benefits over hypodermic needles include cost-effectiveness, rapid onset of action, direct delivery method and improved patient compliance.
The correct administration of a hypodermic needle is crucial for effective treatment as it demands the patient to acquire skills, which can be a tedious practice.

It further impedes patient compliance (Nir et al. In order to overcome this, an intriguing, patient-friendly, and easy-to-administer device referred to as microarray patches came into existence (Giudice and Campbell 20.

MN patches are in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 micron size range, usually less than 1500 µm in length (Nir et al. MNs can circumvent the protective barrier of the SC by piercing the outermost layer of the skin, thereby enabling the attainment of efficient transdermal delivery.
Hydrophilic drugs can be easily incorporated in DMNs, where the dissolution of the polymeric matrix following administration results in the attainment of desirable therapeutic drug concentrations.
However, incorporating hydrophobic drugs into MNs requires the initial formation of drug nanosuspensions, enabling homogenous distribution of the drug.

Nanosuspensions are colloidal dispersions of sub-micron-sized drug particles that are stabilized by the incorporation of stabilizers (Jacob et al. Nanosuspensions, like lipid carrier systems such as liposomes and solid lipid nanoparticles, can be used to formulate lipophilic drugs that possess a high Log P value (Mahajan et al. 2020, 2021; Rojekar et al. There are a few drugs that are insoluble in both water and oil. This can be attributed to its high crystal energy and high melting point, which reduces its ability to undergo dissolution, irrespective of the solvent.
In contrast to lipid carriers, such drugs can also be successfully formulated as nanosuspensions.
The size of such crystalline drug particles is maintained in the sub-micron range (nanocrystals), making it suitable for attaining the desired pharmacokinetic profile (Rabinow 20.
Further, nanosuspensions possess a high drug-loading capacity, owing to their high mass by volume ratio.

This results in better drug delivery efficiency that enables therapeutic drug concentrations at the desired site of action (Huang et al. Therefore, by combining the two concepts of MN-based drug delivery and drug nanonization, effective delivery of poorly water-soluble drugs can be achieved.

Methods of preparation of nanosuspension‑loaded microneedles The preparation of nanosuspension-loaded MNs involves two steps: (i) Fabrication of drug-loaded nanosuspension and (ii) Incorporation of the developed nanosuspension into MN arrays.
The below section discusses in brief, the various methods of preparation of nanosuspensions.
Further, the critical factors and the different ways for its subsequent incorporation into MN patches have been discussed.
The overall performance and the stability of nanosuspensions greatly depend on the method of preparation.
The topdown and bottom-up technologies are the two approaches widely utilized in the preparation of nanosuspensions.
The top-down technology involves the size reduction of larger drug particles into smaller ones by means of various techniques, including milling, high-pressure homogenization and micro fluidization.
In bottom-up technology, the formation Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:475–504 of particles occurs at the molecular level.

The various bottom-up strategies for nanosuspension preparation include a solvent–anti solvent method, supercritical fluid process, spray drying and emulsion–solvent evaporation (Mahesh et al. Top‑down approaches Milling Milling is a widely employed unit operation in pharmaceutical applications for the size reduction of particles.
The particles undergo deformation due to stress imparted by the mechanical energy generated during milling, as shown in of stress applied in mills to reduce particle size.
Wet milling, used in the preparation of nanosuspensions, involves milling a solid suspended in a liquid.
Planetary ball mill and wet stirred media mill are mostly used to produce nanosuspensions.
The particulate material, mixture of solvents, stabilizer and milling beads are fed into the chamber for size reduction.

The milling beads vary in size from 0.1 to 20 mm and are usually made of a complex, and dense material such as stainless steel, glass alumina, yttrium-stabilized zirconium oxide, etc. The beads undergo collision to generate energy that is sufficient for particles to breakdown into a smaller sizes.

The energy generated by the collision of particles and cavitation forces is high enough to cause the comminution of drug particles yielding crystals in the nanosized range.
This technique applies to drugs that exhibit poor solubility in both aqueous and non-aqueous media.
DissoCubes® is the first high-pressure homogenization-based nanocrystal technology that involves the homogenization of drug particles in water.
Later, in the early 2000s, a new technology named Nanopure® was introduced that enables the homogenization of particles in non-aqueous media or in a mixture of water and water-miscible solvents.

High-pressure homogenization is based on the principle of Bernoulli’s theorem, according to which a fall in the static pressure of the liquid below its vapour pressure occurs when the suspension enters the narrow gap that results in the boiling of the fluid.

Once the suspension leaves the gap, an abrupt rise in pressure to normal atmospheric levels causes the vapour bubbles to implode, leading to crystal dislocation, particle collision and subsequent breakdown of particles (Gao et al. The critical variables that affect the physical characteristics of the resultant nanosuspension include the number of homogenization cycles, homogenization pressure, hardness of the drug and the operating temperature (particularly for thermosensitive drugs).
Nanosuspensions produced by high-pressure homogenization possess a broad scope of pharmaceutical applications.

The design of the chamber is such that it divides the nanosuspension into two different streams, which subsequently undergo impingement, causing particle-size reduction.

This reduction in particle size can be attributed to the high-energy impact, cavitation and shear forces generated during the process (Kulshreshtha et al. Microfluidization is performed in Z or Y-type chambers by a jet stream homogenizer.

One distinct advantage of microfluidization over conventional high-pressure homogenization is its less susceptibility to clogging as it operates at a constant shear rate.

Bottom‑up approaches Solvent–anti‑solvent precipitation In the solvent–anti-solvent method, the drug is initially dissolved in a suitable solvent that is followed by the quick addition of an anti-solvent.
This leads to the precipitation of the drug in the form of nanocrystals.
De-solvation upon addition of the anti-solvent leads to supersaturation of drug particles, which subsequently results in precipitation of nano-sized drug particles.
However, since the initially formed particles are unstable, it tends to undergo rapid growth leading to a broad particle-size distribution.

Factors such as the proportion of solvent and anti-solvent, speed of mixing, drug concentration and temperature play a major role in achieving control over the particle size distribution (Du et al. Many drugs have been formulated as nanosuspensions by solvent–anti-solvent precipitation method in order to enhance oral bioavailability (Aukunuru et al. The poor oral bioavailability of the anti-lipidemic drug lovastatin was successfully overcome by formulating it as a nanosuspension using the solvent–anti-solvent precipitation method.

A 2.5-fold increase in bioavailability was achieved with the optimized formulation as compared to the marketed formulation (Patil et al. Further, a novel method of anti-solvent precipitation that avoids the solvent removal step was investigated by Kuk et al. to prepare a nanosuspension of resveratrol using the QbD approach (Kuk et al. In recent times, the solvent–anti-solvent precipitation method has been explored for the preparation of nanosuspensions that are intended for subsequent incorporation into MNs. In a study by Wei et al., DMN arrays containing the hydrophobic drug methotrexate was investigated to improve therapeutic outcomes in rheumatoid arthritis.
The antisolvent precipitation method was used, in which methotrexate was initially dissolved completely in a solvent.

Further, upon addition of the anti-solvent, under stirring, on ice, controlled particle size formation occurred resulting in the formation of nanocrystals with an average particle size of 148.1 ± 10.1 nm and PDI of 0.152 ± 0.024.
To a solution containing the developed nanocrystals, hyaluronic acid and PVP K90 were added and stirred thoroughly.

This solution was then poured into PDMS molds, centrifuged and dried to obtain MN patches with excellent mechanical strength and insertion properties (Wei et al. Factors to be considered for the development of nanosuspension loaded MN In contrast to polymeric or lipidic nanoparticles, nanosuspensions are submicron colloidal dispersions of solid medicines stabilized by a polymer and/or surfactant (Vora et al. For the delivery of -loaded MNs, firstly, the needle must be quickly dissolved in the skin, ideally less than 1 h, to enhance patient compliance.

Several examples of hollow MNs loaded with nanosuspension have been reported in the literature.

Water and other selected excipients, such as the matrix polymer, must not substantially change the properties of the nanoparticles, such as size, charge or aggregation and should not dissolve during manufacturing or storage.
The selected excipient must be biodegradable and should possess a low molecular weight for ready clearance from the body.

The baseplate could be created independently as a polymeric film using wellknown knife-casting methods.
A polymer powder mixture or direct addition of the polymer powder to a concentrated nanosuspension may be necessary to increase drug loading in the MN array's needles.
